outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's well regarded as a piece. It won the 2025 Berggruen Prize essay competition [spya-gp3g6s]. It has also drawn replies, so it's live debate, not superseded. One [LessWrong critique](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/kAHar2hrQbykF9Rt7/contra-anil-seth-on-ai-consciousness) says he doesn't show that life is necessary for consciousness. Another is a [response at Ethics in Review](https://www.ethicsinreview.com/on-anil-seths-the-mythology-of-conscious-ai-part-1/). Seth admits his view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89], which gives your group something to argue about.

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:
You don't need anything first, because the essay explains its own terms. For a group, the useful extras come after it. Seth's follow-up in Noema, [Only What Is Alive Can Be Conscious](https://www.noemamag.com/only-what-is-alive-can-be-conscious), expands his biology argument. The search also found a [thread](https://hraness.com/reading/anil-seth-bbs-conscious-ai-biological-naturalism-thread) about a published collection of 50 commentaries on the essay and his reply to them. I haven't opened either, so check them before you assign them.

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
The byline gives his standing: a neuroscience professor who directs Sussex's Centre for Consciousness Science and wrote "Being You" [spya-rg493b]. He's a credible guide to the science of consciousness. He is also arguing for his own side, and he says so. He admits "I don't have a knock-down argument" [spya-hj5y6s] and that his view "remains a minority view" [spya-qu7j89]. Both passages are good places for your group to push back.

outcomes.text:

outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
I can't judge how well regarded it is from one search, but it's worth your time as an opinionated 2020 essay. It's Gwern's own argument, not a neutral survey. He has followed it up himself in [“Scaling Hypothesis Revisited”](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited) [spya-ewxv9q]. Critiques exist too, such as [“Is the Scaling Hypothesis Falsifiable?”](https://exa.ai/library/publication/wvyyyj4b3l1) and [“Causal confusion as an argument against the scaling hypothesis”](https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/FZL4ftXvcuKmmobmj/causal-confusion-as-an-argument-against-the-scaling). Those pages are only search summaries, and I haven't read them.

Does your group want the technical case or the argument about the critics?

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Gwern Branwen is an independent writer and researcher, not an academic lab member. He describes himself as a [freelance writer and researcher](https://gwern.net/me), and [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/profile?id=%7EGwern_Branwen1) lists him as independent since 2009. This is an advocacy essay. He says he doubted scaling before 2020 and now argues it was right [spya-emqjaa]. Treat his forecasts and his attacks on critics as opinion [spya-zyncdd]. The 2020 numbers are checkable. He later wrote [a revisit](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited), and a [retrospective](https://itdoeswhatnow.com/m/2020-05-28-gwern-publishes-the-scaling-hypothesis/) says Chinchilla later complicated the compute picture.
